Introduction One of the most significant problems facing the environment today is the contamination caused by heavy metals, which is caused by the industrial effluent that is not treated. Because of their recalcitrance, toxicity, and persistence, these heavy metals are a matter of the highest concern (Mohyudin et al., 2022). Industrial effluents and solid urban wastes are a major source of surface water contamination. In industrial areas, the surrounding groundwater gets contaminated by industrial effluents from industries like metal processing, chemical production and paper manufacturing with organic and inorganic contaminants including heavy metals, salts and fluoride (O. Khan et al. 2021). This contaminated water flows through streams, rivers, and wells, eventually ending up in the drinking water system. Although the waste recycling units are limited and not adequate for the treatment of huge load of industrial waste, there are industries which export their waste to other regions. Waste disposal is carried out in most of the units improperly and this has major environmental impacts. The uncontrolled, insufficient, and haphazard management of this waste introduces a significant threat to global environmental health. The environmental matrices are rich with common contaminants that may be very hazardous to both aquatic and terrestrial life (Ali et al., 2021). There are two main categories of environmental pollutants: organic and inorganic. Organic pollutants include common dye compounds like methylene blue that are emitted by factories producing paper, paint, textiles, and other goods. Pesticides, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), phthalate esters (PAEs), bisphenol A (BPA), perfluorinated compounds (PFCs), organic phosphate flame retardants (OFRs), and others are some of the major pollutants (Ali et al., 2018; Ahmad et al., 2021; Clarke and Smith, 2011). Whereas radionuclides and heavy metal ions are examples of inorganic contaminants in wastewater (Rasheed et al., 2022; Ahmad and Mirza, 2018; Mirza and Ahmad, 2018; Zhang et al., 2018; Karaçetin et al., 2014). They have a negative influence on the natural environment and living beings in general due to their carcinogenicity and toxicity. The following are some examples of the maximum permitted levels of heavy metal contaminants: Arsenic: 0.05 mg/l, Cadmium: 0.005 mg/l Lead: 0.015 mg/l, Mercury: 0.002 mg/l, Chromium: 0.1, Selenium: 0.05 mg/l, Antimony: 0.006 mg/l (Rasheed et al., 2022). Since some of them have the ability to bioaccumulate, the damage they do to living organisms may be higher than the harm caused by pollutants that cannot bioaccumulate As a consequence, the deployment of efficient treatment processes for the removal of dangerous toxins has become one of the most significant predictors of long-term industrial success (Rasheed et al., 2022; Berrios et al., 2012; Karaçetin et al., 2014). Thus, it is essential to determine and assess these harmful contaminants from multiple sources, even at low concentration levels (Ali et al., al.2021). Metals including mercury, lead, cadmium, chromium, and arsenic are known to be toxic to humans (Balali-Mood et al., 2021). Many studies have found that cadmium and lead levels in industrial areas were exceed 2 mg/l which is recommended levels by Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986. Despite the fact that the concentrations of heavy metals in water are relatively low, they may have a significant impact on ecosystems and human health after becoming part of the food chain of various species. In this context, concerns about water safety have been raised by researchers due to the increasing detection of these contaminants within water systems, and water quality is seen as a global problem (Am´erico-Pinheiro et al., 2022; Cheng et al., 2021; Mian et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2020). Heavy metals may arise from both natural and human sources and accumulate in several environmental sectors (soil, air, water and its interface). Many studies have shown a variety of natural causes of heavy metal contamination. Metals may be transferred from their endemic spheres into diverse environmental segments through natural weathering processes. Natural heavy metal emissions occur under a variety of environmental situations. Such emissions include rock weathering, sea-salt sprays, volcanic eruptions, biogenic sources, and wind-borne soil particles (Devis et al. 1997; Willis Gwenzi, 2021). According to the findings of a large number of research that have been carried out on the assessment of heavy metals, the principal causes of their contamination in the environment are sources that are anthropogenic. Activities such as agriculture, mining, wastewater treatment, industrial operations, metallurgical processes, and runoffs are examples of some of the activities that contribute to accumulate of heavy metals into different parts of the environment. The major industry sources of heavy metals are summarizes in Table 1. Besides that, Vanadium, selenium, mercury, nickel, and tin are some of the elements that are released when fossil fuels are burnt. Lead is emitted by autos; zinc, arsenic, and copper are emitted by smelting; arsenic is a waste product of pesticides; and automobiles emit lead. All of these human activities account for the most significant contributors to heavy metal accumulation in the environment, and they are the primary anthropogenic causes of heavy metal pollution (Tiwari et al., 2020; Machado et al., 2020). Moreover, the increasing accumulation of several metals in soil and water due to rapid industrialization has posed a worrying situation for humankind and marine life (Patnaik, 2018; Sharma and Rai, 2018; Bakshe and Jugade, 2021). In this experiment, we investigated the effect of mercapto-based palygorskite (MPAL, applied at 2% and 4% w/w) on cadmium (Cd) and lead (Pb) phytostabilization by Chrysopogon zizanioides in soils contaminated with Cd and Pb. The results showed that soil pH did not vary under the application of MPAL but decreased during the cultivation of C. zizanioides. Compared with planting C. zizanioides alone, the application of MPAL significantly promoted the growth of C. zizanioides, enhanced its antioxidant enzyme activities, and decreased Cd and Pb concentrations in roots and shoots. Compared with CK, the addition of 4% MPAL, cultivated with C. zizanioides, reduced DTPA-extracted Cd and Pb in soils by 89.22% and 51.18%, respectively, at the highest level (p < 0.05). Moreover, urease, cellulase, and sucrase activities in soils treated with MPAL and cultivated with C. zizanioides were enhanced, with maximum increases of 37.70%, 110.22%, and 42.99%, respectively (p < 0.05). The interaction of MPAL and C. zizanioides increased bacterial richness and diversity but did not alter the bacterial community. This study demonstrated that the use of MPAL in combination with C. zizanioides could serve as a potential strategy for Cd and Pb immobilization and improvement of soil microecological properties. fetched_contents.text: Molecular Mechanisms of Root Exudate-Mediated Remediation in Soils Co-Contaminated with Heavy Metals and Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons Abstract Soil co-contamination with heavy metals (HMs) and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) represents a widespread and challenging environmental issue that is difficult to address using conventional remediation methods. This review systematically examines the molecular mechanisms by which plant root exudates mediate the remediation of co-contaminated soils through synergistic interactions with rhizosphere microorganisms. We detail how plants dynamically adjust the composition and secretion of root exudates—such as organic acids, amino acids, sugars, and secondary metabolites—in response to combined HM-PAH stress. These exudates play multifaceted roles in remediation, including chelating HMs, enhancing PAH solubility and bioavailability, and acting as chemoattractants and metabolic substrates for rhizosphere microbes. In return, the recruited microbial communities contribute to pollutant detoxification through various mechanisms, such as biosurfactant production, enzymatic degradation, and improved plant nutrient acquisition. This reciprocal interaction forms a synergistic plant-microbe feedback loop that effectively mitigates combined contamination stress. By integrating evidence from diverse plant–soil systems, this review provides a comprehensive mechanistic framework for understanding root exudate-microbe interactions, offering critical insights for developing enhanced phytoremediation strategies to address complex environmental pollution. Keywords: heavy metals, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, root exudates, rhizosphere microorganisms, phytoremediation 1. Introduction Approximately 95% of global food production is derived from terrestrial ecosystems, within which soil plays an indispensable role in the storage, transformation, and recycling of nutrients vital for sustaining human life. As the fundamental bedrock underpinning food security, ecological balance, and human health, healthy soil is essential for achieving sustainable development goals and ensuring environmental security. However, soil health is increasingly threatened by persistent contaminants. Among these, heavy metals (HMs)—such as arsenic (As), cadmium (Cd), chromium (Cr), lead (Pb), and mercury (Hg)—represent a prominent class of inorganic pollutants. Characterized by high density (typically >5 g/cm3), toxicity, and resistance to natural degradation, HMs originate from both natural processes like rock weathering and widespread anthropogenic activities including mining, smelting, industrial discharge, and agricultural practices [1]. Alongside HMs, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) constitute a major group of persistent organic pollutants, primarily formed from the incomplete combustion of fossil fuels and biomass. Their hydrophobic nature, persistence, and potential for bioaccumulation make them a significant environmental concern, with compounds like benzo[a]pyrene (BaP) recognized as highly carcinogenic priority pollutants by the US EPA [2]. According to the United Nations Global Soil Pollution Assessment Report, nearly 500 million hectares of soils worldwide are contaminated, with HMs and PAHs being widespread contributors. While HMs and PAHs differ markedly in their physicochemical properties, their prolonged co-occurrence leads to complex interactions in soil. This results in combined stress effects that are more variable and unpredictable than those from single contaminants, thereby intensifying ecological risks and elevating the threat of irreversible damage to soil structure and function [3,4]. Consequently, the effective remediation of co-contaminated soils has become a pressing global priority. Conventional physicochemical remediation methods often prove inadequate for such complex scenarios, as they can be cost-prohibitive, disruptive to soil structure, and may generate secondary pollution [5]. In contrast, phytoremediation—particularly approaches that leverage the synergistic plant-microbe interactions within the rhizosphere—offers a more sustainable and eco-compatible alternative. The rhizosphere, defined as the narrow soil zone directly influenced by root activity, serves as a dynamic hotspot for biogeochemical processes. Here, plants actively release a diverse and complex mixture of root exudates, including low-molecular-weight organic acids, amino acids, sugars, and secondary metabolites, which collectively reshape the physical structure, chemical equilibrium, and biological functionality of the surrounding soil [6]. These root exudates are not merely passive metabolites; they function as active mediators of plant stress response and key facilitators of in situ remediation. They operate through several interconnected mechanisms: primarily by altering pollutant bioavailability through chelation, solubilization, or precipitation [7]; serving as chemoattractants and metabolic substrates to regulate microbial community composition and activity [6]; and optimizing the rhizosphere microenvironment to favor detoxification processes [8]. This sophisticated chemical dialogue establishes a self-reinforcing plant-microbe feedback loop that is fundamental to the phytoremediation of co-contaminated soils [9]. However, despite these recognized functions, a systematic and mechanistic understanding of how root exudates orchestrate the remediation of combined HM-PAH pollution remains fragmented. Critical knowledge gaps persist regarding the dynamic regulation of exudate profiles under dual stress, the precise molecular mechanisms by which they simultaneously mediate the fate of both inorganic and organic contaminants, and their role in assembling a synergistic, pollutant-degrading microbiome. Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2022 Sep 1. Abstract Abandoned mine lands present persistent environmental challenges to ecosystems and economies; reclamation an important step for overcoming these challenges. Phytostabilization is an elegant and cost-effective reclamation strategy, however, establishing plants on severely degraded soils is problematic, often requiring soil amendment additions. We evaluated whether amendment mixtures composed of lime, biochar, biosolids, and locally effective microbes (LEM) could alleviate the constraints that hinder phytostabilization success. We hypothesized that 1) plants grown in tailings amended with lime, biochar, and biosolids (LBB) would establish faster and grow larger than plants grown in tailings amended with lime only, and 2) the LEM source would influence microbial community function and structure in amended mine tailings. We conducted a greenhouse study that simulated in situ conditions to measure the influence of LBB-LEM amendment blends on plant growth, plant nutrients, metal concentrations, microbial function, and microbial community structure. Blue wildrye [Elymus glaucus Buckley ssp. Jepsonii (Burtt Davy) Gould] was grown in tailings collected from the Formosa mine site amended with various combinations of LBB-LEM. The above and below ground biomass of plants grown in mine tailings amended with LBB was 3 to 4 times larger than the biomass of plants grown in tailings amended only with lime. Although the LEM addition did not influence immediate plant growth, it did affect nutrient content and altered the rhizosphere community membership. As such, it is not yet clear if LEM-driven alterations in microbial membership will advance mine reclamation strategies by improving long-term growth. Keywords: Biochar, phytostabilization, locally effective microbes, mine remediation 1.0. INTRODUCTION Abandoned mine lands (AMLs) pose an ongoing and serious threat to ecosystems, water resources, and human health. In the United States, it is estimated that over 500,000 AMLs contribute to this threat (Bureau of Land Management, 2016; US Government Accountability Office, 2011). The extraction and processing of mineral ore produces copious amounts of waste material, known as tailings. Tailings are often scattered across the surface of mines; eventually, forming deep layers of tailings with extremely low pH, an absence of organic matter, high heavy metal concentrations, poor nutrient-availability, and poor water retention. Collectively, degraded edaphic conditions at AMLs create circumstances that potentiate on- and off-site environmental harm by lowering pH and increasing metal concentrations in adjacent ecosystems (Venkateswarlu et al., 2016). Reclamation strategies that alleviate these on-site issues are desperately required to reduce the incidence of off-site heavy metal movement via water and air erosion into adjacent ecosystems. Attempts to mitigate the environmental threats created by AMLs are often hindered by abiotic constraints and the biotic community that thrives under extreme environmental conditions (Johnson and Hallberg, 2005). One such abiotic constraint is the mineral composition of the tailings, which are typically dominated by pyrite (FeS2). Pyrite is abiotically oxidized in the presence of oxygen to form ferrous iron (Fe2+) and sulfuric acid (Moses et al., 1987). As this reaction proceeds, Fe2+ and sulfuric acid accumulate, and the pH of the system is lowered—conditions that select for the growth and proliferation of iron-oxidizing bacteria (the biotic constraint). In turn, iron-oxidizing bacteria generate ferric iron (Fe3+), which is a more effective oxidant in abiotic pyrite dissolution (Evangelou and Zhang, 1995; Nordstrom et al., 2015; Silverman, 1967). As the tailings weather, the intrinsic connection between the abiotic oxidation of pyrite and microbially-mediated oxidation of Fe2+ accelerates pyrite dissolution. This results in highly acidic tailings (pH ≤ 4) and the generation of acid mine drainage. Thus, efforts to reclaim mine sites must break this cycle by simultaneously addressing the geochemical and the biological factors that contribute to pyrite dissolution (Antonio et al., 2020). Phytostabilization is a reclamation strategy that aims to reduce offsite contaminant movement by establishing plant communities that reduce wind and water erosion of contaminated materials and increase transpiration that reduces infiltration and leaching of contaminants. Increased root biomass stabilizes tailings, reduces erosion, and increases organic matter, which can bind contaminants and improve water retention (Bolan et al., 2011; Mendez and Maier, 2008). Roots also provide habitat and labile carbon for heterotrophic microorganisms, which play a crucial role in nutrient cycling and thereby promote plant growth. Soil microbes are increasingly being recognized as key facilitators of ecological restoration (Harris, 2009), and the development of these communities is critical to phytostabilization success. However, the natural colonization of degraded landscapes occurs on decadal timescales (Grman et al., 2015; Suding et al., 2004), which is unacceptable for remediation projects with time constraints. Previous studies have attempted to accelerate plant root microbial colonization by introducing organic carbon-building soil amendments, such as compost, biochar, and municipal biosolids (Brown et al., 2003; Ippolito et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2012; Ohsowski et al., 2018; Peltz and Harley, 2015; Ye et al., 2000). Mini-report on evidence and field application of phytostabilization

The evidence base shows that phytostabilization has been applied in real-world settings, especially for mining soils and acid mine tailings, with mixed evidence on which contaminants are most successfully stabilized. One recent review says phytostabilization has been widely applied to remediate mining soils contaminated with heavy metals, but high soil toxicity often restricts plant growth and remediation efficiency [N2-F2]. Another study on acidic mine tailings reports that biochar, biosolids, lime, and locally-effective microbes were used to alleviate constraints that hinder phytostabilization success [N4-F4]. These examples suggest field application is strongest where soil toxicity is high or where tailings are severely degraded, rather than in every contaminated site.

The contaminants successfully stabilized in the evidence include cadmium and lead in mining soils [N2-F2], and the study on acidic mine tailings explicitly uses biochar and lime to stabilize tailings chemistry and reduce erosion [N4-F4]. The evidence also indicates that amendments can support plant growth in mine tailings while improving soil properties such as organic matter and water retention [N4-F4]. However, the evidence does not provide a long list of distinct field sites beyond the general categories of mining soils and acid mine tailings, so the strongest supported conclusion is that phytostabilization has been applied in mining environments and degraded tailings rather than in a broad array of specific industrial or agricultural sites.

Performance is measured in practice through several practical indicators. The evidence highlights reduced metal concentrations in roots and shoots when plants are combined with amendments [N2-F2], and reduced DTPA-extracted Cd and Pb in soils as a measure of lower bioavailability [N2-F2]. The tailings study also reports enhanced urease, cellulase, and sucrase activities, which are proxies for improved soil functioning rather than direct metal removal [N2-F2]. In the mine tailings study, plant growth, biomass, and microbial function were also used as performance measures [N4-F4]. Overall, the evidence supports a practical measurement framework centered on metal bioavailability, leaching, and soil chemistry rather than just plant tissue concentrations, which aligns with the idea that phytostabilization targets immobilization rather than extraction [N2-F2].

Tradeoffs between speed, cost, and permanence are evident in the evidence. Phytostabilization is presented as a “cost-effective reclamation strategy” [N4-F4], but it can be slow because natural colonization of degraded landscapes occurs on decadal timescales [N4-F4]. Amendments such as biochar, lime, and biosolids can accelerate plant growth and soil improvement, but they add cost and require management [N4-F4]. The evidence also notes that phytostabilization may not fully remove metals from the soil, so permanence is partly dependent on how well the amendments and plants together reduce bioavailability and prevent erosion [N2-F2][N4-F4]. In short, phytostabilization is attractive when speed is low, cost is a concern, and permanence is less urgent than immediate stabilization; but it is less attractive when rapid cleanup or permanent removal is required [N4-F4].

Overall, the evidence supports phytostabilization as a practical field tool for mining soils and degraded tailings, with performance measured through metal bioavailability, soil enzymes, microbial activity, and plant growth, and with tradeoffs favoring cost and permanence over speed [N2-F2][N4-F4].

Mini-report on limitations, alternatives, and comparison with phytoextraction

The evidence indicates that phytostabilization may fail or be insufficient under several conditions. First, it depends heavily on soil toxicity and plant growth: one review says high soil toxicity often restricts plant growth and remediation efficiency [N2-F2]. Another study on acidic mine tailings notes that severely degraded soils can be difficult to reclaim, requiring amendments to overcome abiotic constraints such as pyrite oxidation and acid mine drainage [N4-F4]. This means phytostabilization may be insufficient where the soil is too acidic, nutrient-poor, or chemically hostile to plant establishment [N4-F4]. Second, the evidence suggests that phytostabilization is not a rapid cleanup method; natural microbial colonization occurs on decadal timescales, which is incompatible with projects needing faster remediation [N4-F4]. Third, the evidence shows that amendments can help, but they do not eliminate the need for careful site-specific management [N4-F4]. In short, phytostabilization is limited when the site is highly degraded, the cleanup deadline is short, or the target metal is not easily immobilized by the available amendments [N2-F2][N4-F4].

Compared with phytoextraction, phytostabilization is fundamentally different. The evidence explicitly contrasts the two approaches: phytoextraction removes metals by concentrating them in shoots for harvest, whereas phytostabilization uses plants to bind and immobilize metals [N5-R4]. A broader review of phytoremediation also notes that phytoextraction is one of the main approaches, while phytostabilization is another [N5-R2]. This distinction is important because phytoextraction is a direct removal strategy, whereas phytostabilization is a containment strategy. The evidence therefore supports phytoextraction when the goal is to extract metals from the soil, whereas phytostabilization is more appropriate when the goal is to reduce metal mobility and prevent off-site movement [N5-R4][N5-R2].

The evidence also briefly mentions other phytoremediation approaches and physical/chemical alternatives. A review notes that phytoremediation can be enhanced by amendments, genetic engineering, and microbial assistance [N5-R2]. Another source indicates that phytoremediation is the direct use of plants for in situ remediation through contaminant removal, uptake, or immobilization [N5-R5]. This implies that physical and chemical methods remain important alternatives when phytostabilization is insufficient or too slow. The mine tailings evidence also emphasizes that phytostabilization is not always sufficient on its own and may need complementary amendments or microbes [N4-F4]. Overall, the evidence suggests that physical and chemical methods are often used when faster or more complete removal is required, while phytostabilization is preferable when the site is degraded, the contamination is widespread, and the goal is sustainable containment rather than rapid extraction [N5-R4][N5-R2][N4-F4].

Site-specific factors matter for choosing phytostabilization over other methods because the evidence repeatedly emphasizes that success depends on soil toxicity, pH, nutrient availability, and the presence of abiotic constraints such as pyrite oxidation [N2-F2][N4-F4]. The acidic mine tailings study also shows that amendments such as biochar, lime, biosolids, and microbes can alter the conditions needed for plant establishment and microbial activity [N4-F4]. In contrast, phytoextraction may be better suited to sites where plant biomass can be harvested and metals concentrated, but not where the soil is too hostile to plant growth [N5-R4]. Therefore, the evidence supports using phytostabilization where the site is degraded, long-term containment is acceptable, and amendments can improve soil conditions; while phytoextraction is better where metals can be concentrated in aboveground biomass and harvested [N2-F2][N5-R4][N4-F4].
node_outputs.N7:
Mini-report on the core mechanism of phytostabilization

The core mechanism of phytostabilization is that plant roots and root exudates alter the soil chemistry near metals without necessarily taking them into plant tissues. The evidence explicitly states that heavy metal ions are stabilized through root exudates without being taken into the root by plants, and that this step is key to phytostabilizing [N3-F3]. It also says that root exudates can trap heavy metal pollutants, which often remain in the soil near the roots, thereby reducing plant damage [N3-R5]. This supports the idea that phytostabilization works through chemical stabilization rather than through uptake into plant tissues [N3-F3][N3-R5].

Plant roots and root exudates alter soil chemistry near metals by modifying the rhizosphere environment. The root-exudate review explains that plants dynamically adjust the composition and secretion of root exudates—such as organic acids, amino acids, sugars, and secondary metabolites—in response to stress [N3-F3]. These exudates function as active mediators of plant stress response and key facilitators of in situ remediation [N3-F3]. They operate through several interconnected mechanisms: altering pollutant bioavailability through chelation, solubilization, or precipitation [N3-F3], serving as chemoattractants and metabolic substrates to regulate microbial community composition and activity [N3-F3], and optimizing the rhizosphere microenvironment to favor detoxification processes [N3-F3]. This means that root exudates are not passive byproducts but active chemical mediators that reshape the local soil chemistry around metals [N3-F3].

Soil processes that immobilize metals include precipitation, adsorption, and complexation. The immobilization evidence says that heavy metals can be retained in the soil through a series of reactions such as adsorption, ionic exchange, and precipitation, forming various metal compounds [N6-R1]. It also notes that soil pH can be altered by amendments such as organic matter, sewage sludge, and others, which can increase soil pH and aid immobilization [N1-R5]. The root-exudate evidence also states that root exudates can trap heavy metals, which remain in the soil near the roots [N3-R5]. Together, this supports the conclusion that immobilization occurs through a combination of chemical reactions and microbial interactions, with adsorption, precipitation, and complexation being the main soil processes [N6-R1][N3-R5].

Metals remain in the soil matrix rather than entering plant tissues because the stabilization is achieved through root exudates and soil chemistry rather than through metal uptake. The evidence explicitly says that heavy metal ions are stabilized without being taken into the root by plants [N3-F3]. It also says that root exudates can trap heavy metal pollutants, which often remain in the soil near the roots [N3-R5]. In addition, the immobilization evidence shows that metals can be retained through adsorption, ionic exchange, and precipitation [N6-R1]. This means the metals are immobilized in the soil, adsorbed onto surfaces, or precipitated as insoluble compounds, rather than transported into the plant’s tissues [N6-R1][N3-F3][N3-R5].

Overall, the core mechanism of phytostabilization is a soil-chemistry-mediated stabilization process: plant roots and exudates alter the rhizosphere, exudates trap metals, and soil processes such as adsorption, precipitation, and complexation immobilize metals in the soil matrix, leaving them largely outside plant tissues [N3-F3][N3-R5][N6-R1].
node_outputs.N10:
Mini-report on plant and amendment traits that enable stabilization

Plant traits that make species suitable for phytostabilization include heavy-metal tolerance, dense root systems, and the ability to support microbial communities. The evidence says that phytostabilization employs heavy metal-tolerant plants, often assisted by soil amendments [N1-R2][N1-R3]. A review also states that phytostabilization is recognized as a gentle remediation option that employs heavy metal-tolerant plants [N1-R2][N1-R3]. Dense root systems are another key trait because they stabilize soil and reduce erosion [N1-R1]. The evidence also emphasizes that roots provide habitat and labile carbon for heterotrophic microorganisms, which play a crucial role in nutrient cycling and thereby promote plant growth [N4-F4]. This means suitable species are not only tolerant of metals but also able to establish dense root systems and support beneficial soil microbes [N1-R2][N1-R3][N4-F4].

Amendments such as lime, biochar, and organic matter improve stabilization by altering soil chemistry and improving plant growth. The evidence notes that organic amendments are often used for phytostabilization of heavy metal-contaminated soils [N1-R4]. It also says that immobilization can be aided by increasing soil pH through amendments such as organic matter, sewage sludge, and others [N1-R5]. The mine tailings study reports that biochar, biosolids, lime, and microbes were used to alleviate constraints that hinder phytostabilization success [N4-F4]. Biochar and lime, in particular, are highlighted as improving acidic soil, supporting microbial nutrient cycles, and enhancing crop growth [N4-R3]. The evidence also indicates that biochar-based amendment blends supported plant growth in mine tailings, with plant growth correlated to increased nutrients but not necessarily increased pH [N4-R1]. Together, these amendments improve stabilization by reducing acidity, increasing organic matter, improving water retention, and promoting microbial activity [N1-R5][N4-F4][N4-R3].

Amendments and plants interact to reduce metal bioavailability through complementary mechanisms. The evidence shows that amendments can alter soil pH, which in turn affects metal solubility and bioavailability [N1-R5]. The root-exudate evidence explains that root exudates can trap heavy metals, which remain in the soil near the roots [N3-R5]. The immobilization evidence adds that metals can be retained through adsorption, ionic exchange, and precipitation [N6-R1]. In the mine tailings study, the combination of biochar, lime, biosolids, and plants enhanced plant growth and microbial activity, and reduced DTPA-extracted Cd and Pb in soils [N2-F2]. This interaction suggests that amendments create favorable soil conditions, while plants and root exudates further immobilize metals in the rhizosphere [N1-R5][N3-R5][N6-R1][N2-F2].

## Summary

Phytostabilization reduces heavy metal pollution by immobilizing metals in the soil matrix rather than taking them into plant tissues. It does this through a combination of plant root activity, root exudates, soil amendments, and chemical processes such as adsorption, precipitation, and complexation. The result is that metals remain near the soil surface, are less available to plants, and are less likely to move offsite through erosion or leaching. This makes phytostabilization especially useful when the goal is long-term containment rather than rapid removal of metals from the soil [N3-F3][N6-R1][N4-F4].

## How phytostabilization works without metal uptake

The core mechanism is that plant roots and root exudates alter the soil chemistry near metals, but the metals themselves do not enter plant tissues in significant amounts. The evidence explicitly states that heavy metal ions are stabilized through root exudates without being taken into the root by plants, and that this step is key to phytostabilizing [N3-F3]. It also says that root exudates can trap heavy metal pollutants, which often remain in the soil near the roots, thereby reducing plant damage [N3-R5]. This means the metals are immobilized locally, not transported into the plant.

The root-exudate evidence explains that plants dynamically adjust the composition and secretion of root exudates—such as organic acids, amino acids, sugars, and secondary metabolites—in response to stress [N3-F3]. These exudates function as active mediators of plant stress response and key facilitators of in situ remediation [N3-F3]. They operate through several interconnected mechanisms: altering pollutant bioavailability through chelation, solubilization, or precipitation [N3-F3], serving as chemoattractants and metabolic substrates to regulate microbial community composition and activity [N3-F3], and optimizing the rhizosphere microenvironment to favor detoxification processes [N3-F3]. In short, root exudates are not passive byproducts but active chemical mediators that reshape the local soil chemistry around metals [N3-F3].

## Which soil processes immobilize metals?

The evidence identifies several soil processes that help immobilize metals:

1. **Adsorption**  
   Heavy metals can be retained in the soil through adsorption and ionic exchange [N6-R1].  
2. **Precipitation**  
   Metals can also be retained through precipitation, forming various metal compounds [N6-R1].  
3. **Complexation**  
   Root exudates can trap heavy metals through complexation, keeping them bound in the soil matrix rather than mobilizing them [N3-R5].  
4. **pH control**  
   Amendments such as organic matter, sewage sludge, and lime can increase soil pH, which in turn aids immobilization [N1-R5].  

Together, these processes reduce the bioavailability of metals and make them less likely to be taken up by plants or transported offsite [N6-R1][N1-R5][N3-R5].

## Why metals remain in the soil matrix rather than entering plant tissues

Metals remain in the soil matrix because the stabilization is achieved through chemical interactions in the rhizosphere rather than through metal uptake into plant tissues. The evidence explicitly states that heavy metal ions are stabilized without being taken into the root by plants [N3-F3]. It also says that root exudates can trap heavy metal pollutants, which often remain in the soil near the roots [N3-R5]. In addition, the immobilization evidence shows that metals can be retained through adsorption, ionic exchange, and precipitation [N6-R1]. This means the metals are immobilized in the soil, adsorbed onto surfaces, or precipitated as insoluble compounds, rather than transported into the plant’s tissues [N6-R1][N3-F3][N3-R5].

The evidence shows that suitable species are not only tolerant of metals, but also have dense root systems and the ability to support microbial communities [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R1]. Dense root systems stabilize soil and reduce erosion, while roots provide habitat and labile carbon for heterotrophic microorganisms, which play a crucial role in nutrient cycling and thereby promote plant growth [N4-F4]. Amendments such as lime, biochar, and organic matter improve stabilization by altering soil chemistry and improving plant growth. The evidence notes that organic amendments are often used for phytostabilization of heavy metal-contaminated soils [N1-R4]. It also says that immobilization can be aided by increasing soil pH through amendments such as organic matter, sewage sludge, and others [N1-R5]. The mine tailings study reports that biochar, biosolids, lime, and microbes were used to alleviate constraints that hinder phytostabilization success [N4-F4]. The evidence also shows that the combination of biochar, lime, biosolids, and plants enhanced plant growth and microbial activity, and reduced DTPA-extracted Cd and Pb in soils [N2-F2]. This interaction suggests that amendments create favorable soil conditions, while plants and root exudates further immobilize metals in the rhizosphere [N1-R5][N3-R5][N6-R1][N2-F2].

The evidence base shows that phytostabilization has been applied in real-world settings, especially for mining soils and acid mine tailings. Overall, the evidence supports a practical measurement framework centered on metal bioavailability, leaching, and soil chemistry rather than just plant tissue concentrations [N2-F2][N4-F4].

Second, the evidence suggests that phytostabilization is not a rapid cleanup method; natural microbial colonization occurs on decadal timescales, which is incompatible with projects needing faster remediation [N4-F4]. Third, the evidence shows that amendments can help, but they do not eliminate the need for careful site-specific management [N4-F4]. In short, phytostabilization is limited when the site is highly degraded, the cleanup deadline is short, or the target metal is not easily immobilized by the available amendments [N2-F2][N4-F4].

Compared with phytoextraction, phytostabilization is fundamentally different. A broader review of phytoremediation also notes that phytoextraction is one of the main approaches, while phytostabilization is another [N5-R2]. This distinction is important because phytoextraction is a direct removal strategy, whereas phytostabilization is a containment strategy. The evidence therefore supports phytoextraction when the goal is to extract metals from the soil, whereas phytostabilization is more appropriate when the goal is to reduce metal mobility and prevent off-site movement [N5-R4][N5-R2].

Another source indicates that phytoremediation is the direct use of plants for in situ remediation through contaminant removal, uptake, or immobilization [N5-R5]. This implies that physical and chemical methods remain important alternatives when phytostabilization is insufficient or too slow. The mine tailings evidence also emphasizes that phytostabilization is not always sufficient on its own and may need complementary amendments or microbes [N4-F4]. Overall, the evidence suggests that physical and chemical methods are often used when faster or more complete removal is required, while phytostabilization is preferable when the site is degraded, the contamination is widespread, and the goal is sustainable containment rather than rapid extraction [N5-R4][N5-R2][N4-F4].

## Why site-specific factors matter

Site-specific factors matter for choosing phytostabilization over other methods because the evidence repeatedly emphasizes that success depends on soil toxicity, pH, nutrient availability, and the presence of abiotic constraints such as pyrite oxidation [N2-F2][N4-F4]. The acidic mine tailings study also shows that amendments such as biochar, lime, biosolids, and microbes can alter the conditions needed for plant establishment and microbial activity [N4-F4]. In contrast, phytoextraction may be better suited to sites where plant biomass can be harvested and metals concentrated, but not where the soil is too hostile to plant growth [N5-R4]. Therefore, the evidence supports using phytostabilization where the site is degraded, long-term containment is acceptable, and amendments can improve soil conditions; while phytoextraction is better where metals can be concentrated in aboveground biomass and harvested [N2-F2][N5-R4][N4-F4].

## Bottom line

Phytostabilization reduces heavy metal pollution without metal uptake by immobilizing metals in the soil matrix through root exudates, adsorption, precipitation, and complexation. Plants and amendments work together to alter soil chemistry, support microbial activity, and reduce metal bioavailability, while the evidence shows that the method is most effective in degraded mining soils and acid mine tailings [N3-F3][N6-R1][N1-R5][N2-F2][N4-F4]. It is a cost-effective, containment-oriented strategy, but it is slower than phytoextraction and may fail when soil toxicity is too high or when rapid cleanup is required [N4-F4][N5-R4]. Overall, phytostabilization is best suited to sites where the goal is long-term reduction of metal mobility and where plant growth and amendments can together stabilize the soil [N1-R2][N1-R3][N4-F4].

## Summary

Phytostabilization reduces heavy metal pollution by immobilizing metals in the soil matrix rather than taking them into plant tissues. It does this through a combination of plant root activity, root exudates, soil amendments, and chemical processes such as adsorption, precipitation, and complexation. The result is that metals remain near the soil surface, are less available to plants, and are less likely to move offsite through erosion or leaching. This makes phytostabilization especially useful when the goal is long-term containment rather than rapid removal of metals from the soil [N3-F3][N6-R1][N4-F4].

## How phytostabilization works without metal uptake

The core mechanism is that plant roots and root exudates alter the soil chemistry near metals, but the metals themselves do not enter plant tissues in significant amounts. The evidence explicitly states that heavy metal ions are stabilized through root exudates without being taken into the root by plants, and that this step is key to phytostabilizing [N3-F3]. It also says that root exudates can trap heavy metal pollutants, which often remain in the soil near the roots, thereby reducing plant damage [N3-R5]. This means the metals are immobilized locally, not transported into the plant.

The root-exudate evidence explains that plants dynamically adjust the composition and secretion of root exudates—such as organic acids, amino acids, sugars, and secondary metabolites—in response to stress [N3-F3]. These exudates function as active mediators of plant stress response and key facilitators of in situ remediation [N3-F3]. They operate through several interconnected mechanisms: altering pollutant bioavailability through chelation, solubilization, or precipitation [N3-F3], serving as chemoattractants and metabolic substrates to regulate microbial community composition and activity [N3-F3], and optimizing the rhizosphere microenvironment to favor detoxification processes [N3-F3]. In short, root exudates are not passive byproducts but active chemical mediators that reshape the local soil chemistry around metals [N3-F3].

## Which soil processes immobilize metals?

The evidence identifies several soil processes that help immobilize metals:

1. **Adsorption**  
   Heavy metals can be retained in the soil through adsorption and ionic exchange [N6-R1].  
2. **Precipitation**  
   Metals can also be retained through precipitation, forming various metal compounds [N6-R1].  
3. **Complexation**  
   Root exudates can trap heavy metals through complexation, keeping them bound in the soil matrix rather than mobilizing them [N3-R5].  
4. **pH control**  
   Amendments such as organic matter, sewage sludge, and lime can increase soil pH, which in turn aids immobilization [N1-R5].  

Together, these processes reduce the bioavailability of metals and make them less likely to be taken up by plants or transported offsite [N6-R1][N1-R5][N3-R5].

## Why metals remain in the soil matrix rather than entering plant tissues

Metals remain in the soil matrix because the stabilization is achieved through chemical interactions in the rhizosphere rather than through metal uptake into plant tissues. The evidence explicitly states that heavy metal ions are stabilized without being taken into the root by plants [N3-F3]. It also says that root exudates can trap heavy metal pollutants, which often remain in the soil near the roots [N3-R5]. In addition, the immobilization evidence shows that metals can be retained through adsorption, ionic exchange, and precipitation [N6-R1]. This means the metals are immobilized in the soil, adsorbed onto surfaces, or precipitated as insoluble compounds, rather than transported into the plant’s tissues [N6-R1][N3-F3][N3-R5].

## How plants and amendments work together to enable stabilization

The evidence shows that suitable species are not only tolerant of metals, but also have dense root systems and the ability to support microbial communities [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R1]. Dense root systems stabilize soil and reduce erosion, while roots provide habitat and labile carbon for heterotrophic microorganisms, which play a crucial role in nutrient cycling and thereby promote plant growth [N4-F4]. This means phytostabilization depends on plant traits that support both soil stabilization and microbial support [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R1][N4-F4].

Amendments such as lime, biochar, and organic matter improve stabilization by altering soil chemistry and improving plant growth. The evidence notes that organic amendments are often used for phytostabilization of heavy metal-contaminated soils [N1-R4]. It also says that immobilization can be aided by increasing soil pH through amendments such as organic matter, sewage sludge, and others [N1-R5]. The mine tailings study reports that biochar, biosolids, lime, and microbes were used to alleviate constraints that hinder phytostabilization success [N4-F4]. Biochar and lime, in particular, are highlighted as improving acidic soil, supporting microbial nutrient cycles, and enhancing crop growth [N4-R3]. The evidence also indicates that biochar-based amendment blends supported plant growth in mine tailings, with plant growth correlated to increased nutrients but not necessarily increased pH [N4-R1]. Together, these amendments improve stabilization by reducing acidity, increasing organic matter, improving water retention, and promoting microbial activity [N1-R5][N4-F4][N4-R3].

Amendments and plants interact to reduce metal bioavailability through complementary mechanisms. Amendments alter soil pH and create favorable conditions for microbial activity, while root exudates trap metals and further immobilize them in the rhizosphere [N1-R5][N3-R5]. The evidence also shows that the combination of biochar, lime, biosolids, and plants enhanced plant growth and microbial activity, and reduced DTPA-extracted Cd and Pb in soils [N2-F2]. This interaction suggests that amendments create favorable soil conditions, while plants and root exudates further immobilize metals in the rhizosphere [N1-R5][N3-R5][N6-R1][N2-F2].

## What field evidence supports phytostabilization?

The evidence base shows that phytostabilization has been applied in real-world settings, especially for mining soils and acid mine tailings. One recent review says phytostabilization has been widely applied to remediate mining soils contaminated with heavy metals, but high soil toxicity often restricts plant growth and remediation efficiency [N2-F2]. Another study on acidic mine tailings reports that biochar, biosolids, lime, and locally-effective microbes were used to alleviate constraints that hinder phytostabilization success [N4-F4]. These examples suggest field application is strongest where soil toxicity is high or where tailings are severely degraded, rather than in every contaminated site [N2-F2][N4-F4].

The contaminants successfully stabilized in the evidence include cadmium and lead in mining soils [N2-F2], and the study on acidic mine tailings explicitly uses biochar and lime to stabilize tailings chemistry and reduce erosion [N4-F4]. The evidence also indicates that amendments can support plant growth in mine tailings while improving soil properties such as organic matter and water retention [N4-F4].

## How performance is measured in practice

In practice, performance is measured through several practical indicators. The evidence highlights reduced metal concentrations in roots and shoots when plants are combined with amendments [N2-F2], and reduced DTPA-extracted Cd and Pb in soils as a measure of lower bioavailability [N2-F2]. The tailings study also reports enhanced urease, cellulase, and sucrase activities, which are proxies for improved soil functioning rather than direct metal removal [N2-F2]. In the mine tailings study, plant growth, biomass, and microbial function were also used as performance measures [N4-F4]. Overall, the evidence supports a practical measurement framework centered on metal bioavailability, leaching, and soil chemistry rather than just plant tissue concentrations [N2-F2][N4-F4].

## Tradeoffs between speed, cost, and permanence

Phytostabilization has clear tradeoffs. It is presented as a cost-effective reclamation strategy [N4-F4], but it can be slow because natural colonization of degraded landscapes occurs on decadal timescales, which is incompatible with projects needing faster remediation [N4-F4]. Amendments such as biochar, lime, and biosolids can accelerate plant growth and soil improvement, but they add cost and require management [N4-F4]. The evidence also notes that phytostabilization may not fully remove metals from the soil, so permanence is partly dependent on how well the amendments and plants together reduce bioavailability and prevent erosion [N2-F2][N4-F4]. In short, phytostabilization is attractive when speed is low, cost is a concern, and permanence is less urgent than immediate stabilization; but it is less attractive when rapid cleanup or permanent removal is required [N4-F4].

## Limitations and comparison with phytoextraction

The evidence indicates that phytostabilization may fail or be insufficient under several conditions. First, it depends heavily on soil toxicity and plant growth: one review says high soil toxicity often restricts plant growth and remediation efficiency [N2-F2]. Another study on acidic mine tailings notes that severely degraded soils can be difficult to reclaim, requiring amendments to overcome abiotic constraints such as pyrite oxidation and acid mine drainage [N4-F4]. This means phytostabilization may be insufficient where the soil is too acidic, nutrient-poor, or chemically hostile to plant establishment [N4-F4]. Second, the evidence suggests that phytostabilization is not a rapid cleanup method; natural microbial colonization occurs on decadal timescales, which is incompatible with projects needing faster remediation [N4-F4]. Third, the evidence shows that amendments can help, but they do not eliminate the need for careful site-specific management [N4-F4]. In short, phytostabilization is limited when the site is highly degraded, the cleanup deadline is short, or the target metal is not easily immobilized by the available amendments [N2-F2][N4-F4].

Compared with phytoextraction, phytostabilization is fundamentally different. The evidence explicitly contrasts the two approaches: phytoextraction removes metals by concentrating them in shoots for harvest, whereas phytostabilization uses plants to bind and immobilize metals [N5-R4]. A broader review of phytoremediation also notes that phytoextraction is one of the main approaches, while phytostabilization is another [N5-R2]. This distinction is important because phytoextraction is a direct removal strategy, whereas phytostabilization is a containment strategy. The evidence therefore supports phytoextraction when the goal is to extract metals from the soil, whereas phytostabilization is more appropriate when the goal is to reduce metal mobility and prevent off-site movement [N5-R4][N5-R2].

The evidence also briefly mentions other phytoremediation approaches and physical/chemical alternatives. A review notes that phytoremediation can be enhanced by amendments, genetic engineering, and microbial assistance [N5-R2]. Another source indicates that phytoremediation is the direct use of plants for in situ remediation through contaminant removal, uptake, or immobilization [N5-R5]. This implies that physical and chemical methods remain important alternatives when phytostabilization is insufficient or too slow. The mine tailings evidence also emphasizes that phytostabilization is not always sufficient on its own and may need complementary amendments or microbes [N4-F4]. Overall, the evidence suggests that physical and chemical methods are often used when faster or more complete removal is required, while phytostabilization is preferable when the site is degraded, the contamination is widespread, and the goal is sustainable containment rather than rapid extraction [N5-R4][N5-R2][N4-F4].

## Why site-specific factors matter

Site-specific factors matter for choosing phytostabilization over other methods because the evidence repeatedly emphasizes that success depends on soil toxicity, pH, nutrient availability, and the presence of abiotic constraints such as pyrite oxidation [N2-F2][N4-F4]. The acidic mine tailings study also shows that amendments such as biochar, lime, biosolids, and microbes can alter the conditions needed for plant establishment and microbial activity [N4-F4]. In contrast, phytoextraction may be better suited to sites where plant biomass can be harvested and metals concentrated, but not where the soil is too hostile to plant growth [N5-R4]. Therefore, the evidence supports using phytostabilization where the site is degraded, long-term containment is acceptable, and amendments can improve soil conditions; while phytoextraction is better where metals can be concentrated in aboveground biomass and harvested [N2-F2][N5-R4][N4-F4].

## Bottom line

Phytostabilization reduces heavy metal pollution without metal uptake by immobilizing metals in the soil matrix through root exudates, adsorption, precipitation, and complexation. Plants and amendments work together to alter soil chemistry, support microbial activity, and reduce metal bioavailability, while the evidence shows that the method is most effective in degraded mining soils and acid mine tailings [N3-F3][N6-R1][N1-R5][N2-F2][N4-F4]. It is a cost-effective, containment-oriented strategy, but it is slower than phytoextraction and may fail when soil toxicity is too high or when rapid cleanup is required [N4-F4][N5-R4]. Overall, phytostabilization is best suited to sites where the goal is long-term reduction of metal mobility and where plant growth and amendments can together stabilize the soil [N1-R2][N1-R3][N4-F4].

## Summary

Phytostabilization reduces heavy metal pollution by immobilizing metals in the soil matrix rather than taking them into plant tissues. It does this through a combination of plant root activity, root exudates, soil amendments, and chemical processes such as adsorption, precipitation, and complexation. The result is that metals remain near the soil surface, are less available to plants, and are less likely to move offsite through erosion or leaching. This makes phytostabilization especially useful when the goal is long-term containment rather than rapid removal of metals from the soil [N3-F3][N6-R1][N4-F4].

## How phytostabilization works without metal uptake

The core mechanism is that plant roots and root exudates alter the soil chemistry near metals, but the metals themselves do not enter plant tissues in significant amounts. The evidence explicitly states that heavy metal ions are stabilized through root exudates without being taken into the root by plants, and that this step is key to phytostabilizing [N3-F3]. It also says that root exudates can trap heavy metal pollutants, which often remain in the soil near the roots, thereby reducing plant damage [N3-R5]. This means the metals are immobilized locally, not transported into the plant.

The root-exudate evidence explains that plants dynamically adjust the composition and secretion of root exudates—such as organic acids, amino acids, sugars, and secondary metabolites—in response to stress [N3-F3]. These exudates function as active mediators of plant stress response and key facilitators of in situ remediation [N3-F3]. They operate through several interconnected mechanisms: altering pollutant bioavailability through chelation, solubilization, or precipitation [N3-F3], serving as chemoattractants and metabolic substrates to regulate microbial community composition and activity [N3-F3], and optimizing the rhizosphere microenvironment to favor detoxification processes [N3-F3]. In short, root exudates are not passive byproducts but active chemical mediators that reshape the local soil chemistry around metals [N3-F3].

## Which soil processes immobilize metals?

The evidence identifies several soil processes that help immobilize metals:

1. **Adsorption**  
   Heavy metals can be retained in the soil through adsorption and ionic exchange [N6-R1].  
2. **Precipitation**  
   Metals can also be retained through precipitation, forming various metal compounds [N6-R1].  
3. **Complexation**  
   Root exudates can trap heavy metals through complexation, keeping them bound in the soil matrix rather than mobilizing them [N3-R5].
